title: The Smallest XOR Sum of a Pairing

concept.title: A bitmask records which elements of b are already used; the number of used elements tells which element of a is next
body: Two lists `a` and `b` of the same length `n` are given. Pair every `a[i]` with a **different** element of `b` (reorder `b` freely) and compute the sum of the XORs of the pairs. What is the **smallest** possible sum? For `a = 1 2` and `b = 2 3` the answer is 2: pair `1` with `3` (XOR 2) and `2` with `2` (XOR 0). Trying all `n!` orders is impossible even for `n = 16` (2 * 10^13).

There are only `2^n` subsets of `b`, so use dynamic programming over the subsets. Assign the elements of `a` **in order**: `a[0]` first, then `a[1]`, and so on. Let `dp[mask]` be the smallest cost of pairing the first `popcount(mask)` elements of `a` with exactly the elements of `b` in the set `mask`. The next element to assign is `a[popcount(mask)]`, and it may be paired with any `b[j]` that is not in the mask: `dp[mask | (1 << j)] = min(dp[mask] + (a[i] ^ b[j]))`, where `i = popcount(mask)`.

The table has `2^n` entries and each is extended in `n` ways, so the work is `n * 2^n = 10^6` for `n = 16`. The answer is `dp` of the full mask. Fixing the order of `a` removes the factor `n!` and keeps the optimal substructure: the cost of the remaining pairs depends only on which elements of `b` are still free.

statement: Two lists `a` and `b`, both of length `n`, are given. Pair each element of `a` with a different element of `b` (a perfect matching). Print the smallest possible sum of `a[i] XOR b[j]` over the pairs.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the length of both lists.
The second line has `n` numbers: the list `a`.
The third line has `n` numbers: the list `b`.

examples.note: The best pairing has the XOR sum 8.

hints: Assign the elements of a one by one in order.
dp[mask] is the cost when the elements of b in mask have been used.
The next element of a has the index popcount(mask).

explanation: dp[mask] is the smallest XOR sum when the first popcount(mask) elements of a are matched with the elements of b in mask; each state is extended by pairing the next element of a with an unused element of b.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
b = list(map(int, input().split()))

inf = 1 << 60
dp = [inf] * (1 << n)
dp[0] = 0
for mask in range(1 << n):
    i = bin(mask).count("1")
    if i == n or dp[mask] == inf:
        continue
    base = dp[mask]
    ai = a[i]
    for j in range(n):
        if not (mask >> j) & 1:
            nm = mask | (1 << j)
            cost = base + (ai ^ b[j])
            if cost < dp[nm]:
                dp[nm] = cost
print(dp[(1 << n) - 1])
